## One function, several methods {#path}

. . .

```julia
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape
    r::Float64
end
struct Rectangle <: Shape
    L::Float64
    w::Float64
end

area(c::Circle)    = π * c.r^2
area(r::Rectangle) = r.L * r.w

area(Circle(2.0))             # Python OOP: shape.area()
```

. . .

> A function can have several **methods**. Argument types determine which method is called.

::: {.notes}
20-minute core, session 1 minutes 150–170. Explain how type information affects compiled code.
▶ Script: cell "1. One function, several methods". Start directly from the definitions.
Shape is abstract: Circle and Rectangle are its concrete subtypes. Do not contrast method
ownership or syntax as a performance explanation. Next: multiple arguments, then when a call
can be resolved. Python exercises are optional for this short language-specific module.
:::

## Dispatch uses all argument types

. . .

```julia
collide(a::Circle,    b::Circle)    = "two circles"
collide(a::Circle,    b::Rectangle) = "circle and rectangle"
collide(a::Rectangle, b::Rectangle) = "two rectangles"

collide(Circle(1.0), Rectangle(2.0, 3.0))
```

. . .

> If we swap the arguments, is the corresponding method defined?

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "2. Dispatch uses all argument types". Argument order is significant:
(::Rectangle, ::Circle) is distinct from (::Circle, ::Rectangle). The reverse pair is not
currently defined; Julia does not assume symmetry. The optional appendix shows its error and fix.
Ordinary Python method lookup for a.collide(b) uses a; handling b requires additional logic.
That logic can be implemented with conditionals, external functions or dispatch libraries.
:::

## When can the compiler resolve the call?

. . .

```julia
circles = [Circle(r) for r in rand(1000)]
concrete = circles                         # Vector{Circle}
abstract_elements = Shape[c for c in circles]  # Vector{Shape}

total(v) = sum(area, v)
```

. . .

Same circles, different element types. **Which call is faster?**

```julia
total(concrete)
total(abstract_elements)
```

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "3. Same values, different element types". Collect predictions before running
the timing cell. Both arrays contain only circles; abstract_elements is not heterogeneous.
The Shape annotation changes the declared element type, not the values. The same Circle values
are reused rather than regenerating radii. Verify the two totals before interpreting timings.
:::

## Same values, different performance

. . .

Reference observation, 1000 circles, warmed-up calls on the course laptop:

| Element type | Time | Calls inside the loop |
|---|---|---|
| `Circle` | ~0.1 µs | Resolved and inlined in this example |
| `Shape` | ~1 µs | Dynamic method calls remain |

. . .

> A concrete element type helps the compiler **resolve calls inside the loop**.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cells "Measure the two containers" and "Inspect calls inside the loop".
Historical rounded BenchmarkTools minimum timings; both versions allocated zero bytes in that
run. The observed speedup is about 10×, not a guaranteed penalty for abstract types.
Inspect @code_typed: a dynamic call to area survives for Vector{Shape}. Type information also
allows inlining and other optimizations. Abstract types are useful for generic interfaces;
this experiment concerns abstract element storage in a performance-critical loop.
:::

## Global variable or argument?

. . .

```julia
glob = rand(1000)    # non-constant global, without a type annotation
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
function sum_global()
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(glob)
        s += glob[i]
    end
    return s
end
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
function sum_arg(x)
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
```
:::
::::

. . .

> Same data: predict the time and allocations of each version.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "4. Global variable or argument". The qualification matters: this is a
non-constant, untyped global. Do not generalize to constants or annotated globals.
Use sum_arg(glob) to hold the input fixed. The result must agree before comparing timings.
:::

## Which types could the compiler infer?

. . .

Selected types from `@code_warntype`:

| | `sum_global()` | `sum_arg(glob)` |
|---|---|---|
| Input | `glob::Any` | `x::Vector{Float64}` |
| Accumulator | `s::Any` | `s::Float64` |
| Return | `Body::Any` | `Body::Float64` |

. . .

Reference: **~118 µs, ~4000 allocations** versus **~0.92 µs, 0 allocations**.

> Unknown types can require **dynamic calls inside the loop**.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cells "Inspect inferred types" and "Measure global and argument versions".
Historical rounded times on the course laptop, warmed-up calls. Inspect the loop's types,
not only the output color. The complete diagnostic stays in the script and notebook.
In this example dynamic indexing/arithmetic and boxing contribute to both time and allocations.
An argument lets Julia specialize for the supplied array type. The ratio is an observation,
not a general claim about Python or about every global variable.
:::

## Keep types visible to the compiler

- Pass working data as **function arguments**.
- Prefer **concrete element types** in performance-critical loops.

. . .

Measure first; inspect inferred types when needed.

. . .

[Script](../scripts/2_dispatch_vs_oop.jl) · [Julia notebook](../pluto/2_dispatch_vs_oop.jl) · [Python examples](../python/2_dispatch_vs_oop_python.ipynb) · [Optional activity](../activities/release/2_dispatch_julia_todo.jl)

::: {.notes}
Two practical rules, not a requirement to annotate every argument with a concrete type.
A generic method such as area(c::Shape) can still specialize on its actual argument type.
The issue illustrated above is unknown types inside a hot loop, not generic interfaces.
@btime mysum($v) supplies the input value rather than including global lookup in the benchmark.
Later, array argument types select the GPU implementation of the same mathematical operation.
:::

# Optional dispatch examples {#appendix style="text-align: center;"}

## The missing argument pair

. . .

```julia
collide(Rectangle(1.0, 1.0), Circle(2.0))
```

What happens? How would you declare symmetry?

. . .

`MethodError`: no method matches `(::Rectangle, ::Circle)`.

```julia
collide(a::Rectangle, b::Circle) = collide(b, a)
```

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cells "5. Optional — the missing argument pair" and "Declare the reverse pair".
An undefined combination fails when called. This does not provide a static coverage check.
In Pluto the reverse-pair definition is disabled until the instructor enables it; otherwise
reactivity would make the earlier error disappear before it can be discussed.
:::

## A new operation on existing types

. . .

```julia
perimeter(c::Circle)    = 2π * c.r
perimeter(r::Rectangle) = 2 * (r.L + r.w)

perimeter.([Circle(2.0), Rectangle(3.0, 4.0)])
```

. . .

> Add methods for a new operation without changing the type definitions.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "A new operation on existing types".
With class-defined methods, the operation is added to each relevant class. Python also offers
external functions and singledispatch; the Python notebook gives an example. Neither arrangement
alone establishes a performance difference. Visitor and the expression problem are out of scope.
:::

```julia

```
